results.title: pashupatinath
results.text: It's very important to visit this temple for Hindus.This was my 3rd visit. There were huge crowds but it is managed well now & could take the darshan from four doors easily.

results.title: Not much to see for 1000 rupees
results.text: If you have been to Varansi to see public cremations and Sadhu, this temple is not worth paying 1000 rupees. You are not allowed inside the Hindu Temple except for the grounds outside the temple.  There wasn't much to see and we spent less than half hour wandering around. On the other side was one public cremation and a couple of Sadhus walking around.

results.title: A Fascinating Place
results.text:
As you can read in the other reviews, this is a place that will spark a lot of thought and reflection.  Yes, you do see bodies in various stages of the cremation process and you most likely will be able to view a funeral ceremony/ritual.  We had a guide with us and he was vital to helping us understand each aspect of the process.

We entered the site from the back and took the long steps up to the cremation view-point.  I highly recommend this route as you can see the deer in the adjacent park; the monkeys all along the way; and the various shrines at the top of the stairs.  Many folks who came from the other entrance missed this area.

Note: You may wish to bring a breath mask or bandana along as the smoke from the cremations tends to blow right across the river.

results.title: An eye-opener
results.text: I really did not fancy visiting a cremation site but how wrong I was.  I came away with a far greater understanding and huge respect for the Hindu tradition.  It is busy, there are lots of hawkers and tourists but there are also many local people just soaking up the atmosphere as we did.

results.title: Hindu Temple
results.text: This Hindu temple is quite a sight.  Surrounding the temple, you will encounter monkeys, wandering cows, hawkers, the holy men and incense smell for starters. Then you will witness the Hindu cremation rituals. When you go up the first set of stairs be sure to stop and take photos behind you.  The view is amazing and the best place. The ground tapers off past this point. The other best picture op is through the doorway of the line of temples open on all sides.

results.title: Not for the faint-hearted
results.text: If you don't want to see bodies being cremated in the open air then stay away. In the west we hide death behind curtains, in Nepal the don't and in Pashupatinath temple you get very much face to face with death.

results.title: Not too intresting
results.text: The entrance is quite high at 1,000 rupees and you cant go into the temple proper . You can only stand on the other side of the river to watch a funeral ceremony and the cremation which is next to the river which at the time of writing is dry. Better to go with a guide.

results.title: Very precious Hindu temple
results.text: Pashupatinath temple purely related to the Hindus is the holy temple for them. It is the temple indicating lord Shiva( The Destroyer) according to the Hindu epics. He had home here in the bank of Bagmati river so as it is also situated in the bank of Bagmati river. This temple is very old about 300 years old. You will also have to pay some entry fees to go inside. You can see the splendid artitecture of the temple and lies north east of Kathmandu

results.title: Interesting
results.text: Its a great temple, worth one visit, though lots of monkeys around! Some even took the chanas I was eating...ha ha. But  enjoyed the visit...

results.title: Cremation ceremony up close and personal
results.text: I was surprised that the tourist ticket was really high compared to other places in Ktm but it was worth it! Go to where they do the cremation process. I was quite shocked at how close it was to the spectators. A guide I "accidentally" hired explained a lot of the history of the place, I think it was well worth-it.

results.title: Somewhat uncomfortable, but interesting
results.text: The temple itself can only be peered at from across the river - for non-Hindus that is. the cremations can be confronting, take a scarf with you to cover your face as the smoke will find you at some point! We wandered around for a while, went up the hill to the small little temples, it was fun to talk to the 'holy' men who will charge money to have a photo with you. Additionally we walked around the market, very colorful! Beware the friendly locals wanting to tell you all about it they are tour guides and expect to be paid, clarify a price before they lead you anywhere.

results.title: Well worth a visit.
results.text: Hindu sacred place. Shrines, temples and burial by the lake (the smell of the smoke was thick in the vicinity of the fires). But very interesting to see.

results.title: Temple & Bagmati River
results.text: We caught the taxi from Kathmandu to the town it cost 400 rupees and he dropped us of right at the ticket booth. Tickets are 1000 rupees each however you are no allowed into the temples unless you are hindu so you are left with walking around the streets and the opposite side of the river where the cremations take place. It is interesting to see the different rituals occur, there are lots of people offering guiding services too. There are plenty of sadhus in all sorts of colourful dress and body painting willing to have their photo taken. Please be respectful of the families mourning and don't take intrusive photographs. We walked to the next town to the Bodnaht Stupor & caught a taxi back to Thamel 500 rupees but it is possible to catch a local bus

results.title: It felt like gate-crashing a funeral
results.text:
I did not enjoy my visit. 
As a non-Hindu, I felt uncomfortable, for two reasons. Firstly, we are not allowed into the temple and it has to be viewed from outside, across the river. Truth said, there is not much to see other than a large structure, which is not as attractive as a number of others in & around Kathmandu. 
Secondly, there were a number of cremations going on, and apart from the fact that I have no desire to see one, it felt offensive to be spectators to such an intimate and sorrowful event.
Thirdly, the surroundings are dreadful: the river Bagmati is horribly polluted with sewerage and general rubbish (smelly) and there are a number of mangy dogs lurking about (would they bite?). The buildings are not well looked after and the general ambiance is jaded and slovenly.
Lastly there are a number of "sadhus" that loiter about looking very grand in all their finery and painted faces, extorting money from foreigners to have their photos taken. They didn't strike me as the real thing at all (and I have heard that indeed they aren't!). Just for show!
I appreciate that this is a Hindu holy site, and thus respect the way they maintain its function. I feel the whole site should be closed to foreigners. Don't leave us to be gawkers treating it as a sight-seeing opportunity.

results.title: Temple and outdoor crematorium
results.text:
It's hard to explain this place.

The first thing you do is to pay 1000 rupees (around 10$) to get in. It's a high price because non-hindus can not get into the temple, but if you surround it and go towards the river, you will see the crematory in the middle of the river. Outdoor crematorium where tourists pay to get in, is in itself, a bit extreme.

When we went there were seven or eight funeral pyres. Some were finishing, other ones were just arriving. The smell, the river, the fire... everything is shocking.

We went with young kids, and of course we had to explain before reaching the place, and of course during the staying. I have to say it was a very good conversation with my daughter.
